entities.name: Temple of Ellesyia
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Temple of Ellesyia (Italian: Tempio di Ellesija) is an ancient Egyptian rock-cut temple originally located at Ellesija in Nubia (now submerged under Lake Nasser following the construction of the Aswan High Dam in the 1960s-1970s), dedicated primarily to Pharaoh Thutmose III (ruled 1479-1425 BCE) and to the gods Horus and Satet — and saved from the dam's flooding through the Italian government's UNESCO rescue effort, with the temple dismantled, transported to Turin, Italy, and reassembled in the Museo Egizio (Egyptian Museum of Turin), where it stands as one of the most unusual museum objects in the world: an entire ancient Egyptian temple rebuilt inside a museum.

The Temple of Ellesija dates to the New Kingdom (approximately 1430 BCE) and was carved directly into the sandstone cliffs of the Nubian Nile. Rock-cut temples were characteristic of Egyptian Nubian sacred architecture — the most famous examples being the Abu Simbel temples of Ramesses II. Ellesija's temple, though smaller, reflects the same architectural approach: creating sacred space within the living rock of a Nile cliff, with the inner sanctuary oriented to catch the rising sun's rays on specific sacred days.

The 1960s UNESCO Nubia Campaign to save monuments threatened by the Aswan High Dam's flooding was one of the largest international heritage rescue operations in history. Egypt and Sudan offered rescued monuments to contributing nations — Italy received Ellesija for its early contributions. The temple was dismantled block by block, transported to Turin, and reassembled in a specially designed gallery in the Museo Egizio. The Museo Egizio itself is the world's largest Egyptian museum outside Egypt, making Ellesija's display context extraordinary — an authentic ancient Nubian rock temple inside Italy's premier Egyptian collection.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Temple of Ellesija — saved by the landmark UNESCO Nubia Campaign, reassembled as a complete ancient Egyptian Nubian rock temple inside Turin's Museo Egizio, and documenting Thutmose III's Nubian building program — is historically significant for both its Egyptian content and as a monument to 20th-century international heritage rescue.
